title: The first sign (John 2:1–12)
hookLine: John calls miracles signs: six stone jars of water become the best wine
carry: the best was kept till last

cards: The third day, John says, there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee. A wedding, a crowded house, a family hosting everyone they know. And partway through the celebration, the thing no host wants happens.
The wine runs out. Jesus is there with his new disciples, and so is his mother, and she's the one who notices. She comes to him and says, simply, in the King James words: "They have no wine."
No request. Just the problem, laid in front of her son.

teach.b: His answer sounds sharp in English: "Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come." But some readers hear more respect in it than English allows, and he uses the same word for her later, from the cross.
His hour keeps coming back in this Gospel, pointing toward the cross and his glory. And his mother doesn't argue.
She turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it."

teach.h: SIX JARS, FILLED TO THE BRIM.
teach.b: Nearby stand six stone water jars, set there, John says, for the Jewish rites of purifying, each holding two or three firkins, the King James says. Big jars.
Fill them with water, Jesus says, and they fill them to the brim. Draw some out now, and take it to the master of the feast.

He tastes it, has no idea where it came from, and calls over the bridegroom: "Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now."
Six jars of the best wine, at the end of a party.
Then John tells us what kind of story this is: "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him."
The King James says miracles, but John's Greek word is sēmeion: sign. Not a show of power for its own sake.
A sign isn't the destination; it points beyond itself.

teach.h: THOU HAST KEPT THE GOOD WINE UNTIL NOW.
teach.b: Some Christians have read this one as pointing to abundance, to joy, to a wedding feast at the end of time, to something better saved for last.

how: Some lectionaries set the wedding at Cana in the weeks after Epiphany, some couples choose it for their weddings, and in the Catholic rosary it is one of the luminous mysteries.

o: a prophecy that tells when the world will end
a miracle that points beyond itself to Jesus
a mark God puts on a person's forehead

games.q: what's inside John 2:1–12 — tap the pairs.
p: his mother lays out the problem
his mother's word to the servants
for washing, filled to the brim
sign: a work that points beyond

s: Jesus calls his mother 'woman' only at Cana
he uses the same word for her again from the cross.
John's word for Jesus's miracles is 'sign'
semeion. Cana is 'this beginning' of the signs.
the master of the feast knew where the wine came from
he didn't know. the servants who drew the water knew.

games.q: you're a servant at the wedding. the wine is gone. Jesus's mother tells you to do whatever he says, and he says to fill six huge jars with water. what do you do?
o: fill them halfway, just in case.
go looking for more wine instead.
games.why: they filled them up to the brim. the water drawn out was the best wine of the feast.

practice: Look around wherever you are and find one ordinary thing, a cup, a ring, a photo, light on a wall, and let your eyes rest on it. Ask what it points to, a person, a promise, a memory, a hope, and stay with that a while.
If you pray, you can give thanks for what it points to.

wordCard.voice: Sign. John's word for Jesus's miracles: not just wonders, but things that point beyond themselves, John says, to who Jesus is. Cana is the first.

orig.note: Greek: a sign, a mark, a token. John's word for Jesus's miracles, translated 'miracles' in the King James.

carryVoice: Your line: the best was kept till last. And the first sign came at a wedding. See you tomorrow.
